_readme: Botswana facts shown on the game-over card, one each finished game, never repeating until all have been shown. Edit freely: keep ids unique and stable (add new ids at the end); FactsTest checks count, uniqueness and length.

facts.text: Botswana is landlocked and borders South Africa, Namibia, Zimbabwe and Zambia.
Botswana and Zambia touch at a single point on the Zambezi near Kazungula, one of the shortest borders in the world.
Botswana covers about 582,000 km², roughly the size of France.
The Kalahari covers around 70% of Botswana's land.
Most of Botswana's people live in the east, along the railway line from Lobatse to Francistown.
Botswana's highest point is Otse Hill (Monalanong), about 1,490 m above sea level.
Botswana's lowest point is where the Shashe River meets the Limpopo, about 510 m above sea level.
The Limpopo River forms part of Botswana's border with South Africa.
The Chobe River forms part of Botswana's northern border with Namibia.
Botswana sits on a high plateau; most of the country lies around 1,000 m above sea level.
The Tropic of Capricorn passes through Botswana, just south of Mahalapye.
Botswana has a semi-arid climate with hot summers and cool, dry winters.
Botswana's rains fall mostly between November and March.
Winter nights in the Kalahari can drop below freezing even though the days are warm.
Botswana is divided into districts such as Central, Ghanzi, Kgalagadi, Kgatleng, Kweneng, North-East, North-West, South-East and Southern.
The Central District is Botswana's largest district by area.
The Kazungula Bridge over the Zambezi, linking Botswana and Zambia, opened in 2021.
Lake Ngami, south of the Okavango, fills and dries with the floods; David Livingstone reached it in 1849.
The Boteti River carries Okavango overflow towards the Makgadikgadi Pans.
The Boteti River stopped flowing for years and returned with strong floods around 2009.
The Gcwihaba (Drotsky's) Caves in north-west Botswana are known for their stalactites and bats.
The Aha Hills sit on Botswana's border with Namibia in the north-west.
The Tsodilo Hills rise abruptly from the flat Kalahari sands in the north-west.
Botswana has no coastline, yet the Okavango is one of Africa's great wetlands.
The Shashe River flows past Francistown on its way to the Limpopo.
The Notwane River runs past Gaborone and feeds the Limpopo system.
Gaborone Dam, on the Notwane River, supplies water to the capital.
The North-South Carrier pipeline carries water from dams in the north-east to Gaborone.
Kalahari sand can be more than 100 m deep in places.
The Linyanti swamps lie in the far north, along the Namibian border.
Botswana is one of the most sparsely populated countries in Africa.
Botswana's 2022 census counted about 2.4 million people.
Fossil river valleys called mekgacha cross the Kalahari, a sign of wetter times.
Dust devils are common on the open pans on hot afternoons.
The Mababe Depression, between Savuti and Moremi, is the bed of an ancient lake.
The Okavango River rises in the highlands of Angola, where it is called the Cubango.
The Okavango Delta never reaches the sea; its water spreads into the Kalahari and evaporates.
The Okavango Delta became UNESCO's 1,000th World Heritage Site in 2014.
The Okavango floods peak in Botswana's dry winter, months after the rain falls in Angola.
Flood water can take about four months to travel from the top of the Okavango to Maun.
The Okavango Delta is listed under the Ramsar Convention as a wetland of international importance.
The Okavango Panhandle is the narrow channel where the river enters Botswana near Shakawe.
Most of the water entering the Okavango Delta is lost to evaporation and plant transpiration.
Islands in the Okavango often start as termite mounds that trees and soil build on.
Chief's Island is the largest island in the Okavango Delta and lies in Moremi Game Reserve.
A mokoro is a dugout canoe poled through the shallow channels of the Okavango.
Mokoro polers stand at the back and push with a long pole called a ngashi.
Many safari mekoro are now made of fibreglass to save the trees once used to carve them.
Papyrus lines the deep, permanent channels of the Okavango.
The Okavango's water is so clear in places that you can see the riverbed.
The Okavango Delta covers several thousand square kilometres of permanent and seasonal swamp.
Maun, on the Thamalakane River, is the gateway town for Okavango safaris.
The Okavango Delta is home to the Bayei, Hambukushu, Bataweng and other peoples.
The Bayei are known as skilled mokoro builders and fishermen of the Okavango.
Water lilies bloom across the Okavango's lagoons and channels.
The Okavango Delta supports large populations of elephants, buffalo, lechwe and hippos.
The sitatunga antelope lives in the Okavango's papyrus swamps and is an excellent swimmer.
Red lechwe use their long, splayed hooves to run through shallow water.
The Okavango is one of the largest inland deltas in the world.
Scenic flights over the Okavango show its maze of channels, lagoons and islands.
The Thamalakane River at Maun fills with water from the Okavango floods.
Xakanaxa and Third Bridge are well-known camping areas in Moremi.
Moremi Game Reserve covers much of the eastern Okavango Delta.
Moremi Game Reserve was declared in 1963 by the BaTawana, one of the first reserves in Africa created by local people.
Moremi Game Reserve is named after Kgosi Moremi III of the BaTawana.
The Okavango Delta's wildlife moves with the floods, crowding onto islands when the water is high.
Fish such as tigerfish and bream draw anglers to the Okavango Panhandle.
Chobe was Botswana's first national park, proclaimed in 1968.
Chobe National Park has one of the highest concentrations of elephants in Africa.
Botswana has the largest elephant population in the world, roughly 130,000 animals.
Chobe's Savuti area is known for lions that hunt elephants.
The Savuti Channel flows only in some years, then dries up for long periods.
Kasane is the main town for visitors to Chobe National Park.
Boat safaris on the Chobe River bring visitors close to drinking elephants.
Sedudu Island in the Chobe River was ruled Botswana's by the International Court of Justice in 1999.
The Chobe riverfront is busiest with game in the dry season, when inland water runs out.
Chobe's Linyanti area is known for wild dogs and large elephant herds.
Chobe National Park covers about 11,700 km².
Kazungula, near Kasane, is where four countries almost meet: Botswana, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Victoria Falls in Zimbabwe is only about 80 km from Kasane.
The Chobe River joins the Zambezi near Kazungula.
Puku, a rare antelope in Botswana, can be seen along the Chobe floodplains.
The Chobe Enclave is a group of villages beside the park where people live with wildlife.
Elephants in Chobe swim across the river and use their trunks as snorkels.
Kasane has a giant baobab once used as a prison cell.
The Central Kalahari Game Reserve was established in 1961.
The Central Kalahari Game Reserve covers about 52,800 km², larger than the Netherlands.
Deception Valley in the Central Kalahari was home to researchers Mark and Delia Owens, authors of Cry of the Kalahari.
The Kalahari is a semi-desert: it gets more rain than a true desert and is covered in grass and scrub.
The Kalahari is famous for its black-maned lions.
After good rains, the Kalahari pans fill with springbok, gemsbok and wildebeest.
The Khutse Game Reserve lies just south of the Central Kalahari Game Reserve.
The Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park joins Botswana's Gemsbok National Park and South Africa's Kalahari Gemsbok National Park.
The Kgalagadi Transfrontier Park was opened in 2000 as Africa's first formally declared transfrontier park.
The Kalahari's red dunes are coloured by a coating of iron oxide on the sand grains.
Tsamma melons store water and help people and animals survive in the Kalahari.
The Makgadikgadi Pans are among the largest salt flats in the world.
The Makgadikgadi Pans are the remains of an ancient lake that once covered much of northern Botswana.
Ntwetwe and Sowa (Sua) are the two biggest pans of the Makgadikgadi.
Kubu Island, a granite outcrop on Sowa Pan, is ringed by baobabs.
Kubu Island is a national monument and a sacred site.
Kubu means hippopotamus in Setswana.
Sowa Pan fills with water in good rainy seasons and attracts huge flocks of flamingos.
Both greater and lesser flamingos breed on Sowa Pan.
The Nata Bird Sanctuary on the northern edge of Sowa Pan was set up by the local community.
Each year zebras migrate between the Boteti River and the Makgadikgadi pans.
A zebra migration of about 500 km between Namibia's Chobe floodplain and Nxai Pan was recorded in 2014, among Africa's longest.
Nxai Pan National Park lies north of the Makgadikgadi and is known for wet-season zebra herds.
Baines' Baobabs, on Kudiakam Pan in Nxai Pan National Park, were painted by Thomas Baines in 1862.
Baines' Baobabs are also called the Sleeping Sisters.
Chapman's Baobab, a famous Makgadikgadi landmark, fell in 2016.
Green Kalahari grass after rain can turn the pans into a short-lived grazing paradise.
Soda ash and salt are extracted from Sowa Pan at Botash, near Sowa Town.
Stone tools found around the Makgadikgadi show people lived there long ago.
Brown hyenas forage along the edges of the Makgadikgadi Pans.
Meerkat groups near the Makgadikgadi have become used to people and can be watched close up.
On a dry pan, mirages make the horizon seem to shimmer with water.
Makgadikgadi Pans National Park borders the Boteti River on its west.
Quad bikes once crossed the pans in the dry season; the salt crust stays fragile and easily damaged.
The Kalahari is shared by Botswana, Namibia and South Africa.
Camelthorn trees (mogotlho) are a common sight in the Kalahari.
Ghanzi, in the western Kalahari, is a centre of cattle ranching.
Kalahari truffles appear in the sand after good rains.
The Kalahari's sand ridges run in long parallel lines, shaped by ancient winds.
The zebra is Botswana's national animal.
The kori bustard, one of the world's heaviest flying birds, is often called Botswana's national bird.
Botswana is home to Africa's Big Five: lion, leopard, elephant, buffalo and rhino.
The Khama Rhino Sanctuary near Serowe was set up by the community in 1992 to protect rhinos.
Rhinos were reintroduced to the Okavango after poaching wiped them out there.
Northern Botswana is one of the last strongholds of the African wild dog.
African wild dogs are also called painted wolves for their patchy coats.
Cheetahs live across Botswana's open plains and the Kalahari.
Brown hyenas, rare in much of Africa, live in the Kalahari.
Gemsbok can go for long periods without drinking, getting water from plants.
Springbok are famous for pronking: leaping high with a stiff-legged bounce.
Meerkats stand guard on their hind legs while the group feeds.
The aardvark digs burrows that many other animals later use.
Pangolins, among the world's most trafficked animals, live in Botswana.
The honey badger is famous for its fearless temper.
Bat-eared foxes use their huge ears to hear insects underground.
Elephants in Botswana can drink well over 100 litres of water a day.
An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscles.
Elephants use their feet to sense rumbles sent by other elephants.
Hippos can stay under water for several minutes before surfacing to breathe.
Hippos leave the water at night to graze on land.
Nile crocodiles live in the Okavango, Chobe and Limpopo rivers.
Lions in the Okavango have learnt to swim between islands.
Leopards often drag their prey into trees to keep it from hyenas and lions.
A giraffe's tongue can be about 45 cm long.
Giraffes in Botswana often feed on acacia trees despite their thorns.
Buffalo herds in northern Botswana can number in the hundreds.
The roan and sable antelope live in northern Botswana's woodlands.
Kudu bulls have long spiral horns that can reach well over a metre.
The steenbok is a small antelope that lives alone or in pairs.
Impala leap high when startled, confusing predators.
Warthogs kneel on their front legs to graze.
Blue wildebeest once migrated in great herds across the Kalahari.
Veterinary fences built to protect cattle have blocked old wildebeest migration routes in Botswana.
Chacma baboons are common in the Okavango and Chobe.
Vervet monkeys are often seen around camps in northern Botswana.
Spotted hyenas are skilled hunters, not just scavengers.
The caracal can leap high to catch birds in flight.
Ground squirrels in the Kalahari use their bushy tails as sunshades.
The black mamba is one of Botswana's most feared snakes.
The African rock python is Africa's largest snake and lives in Botswana.
Mopane worms are caterpillars of the emperor moth that feed on mopane trees.
Termite mounds in Botswana can stand several metres tall.
Dung beetles roll balls of dung that they use for food and egg laying.
Botswana's wildlife areas cover a large share of the country.
Elephants push over trees to reach leaves and roots, shaping the savanna.
Botswana's tsessebe is among the fastest antelope in Africa.
Waterbuck have a white ring on their rump.
Bushbuck are shy antelope that live in riverine thickets.
The serval has the longest legs for its body size of any cat.
Elands are the largest antelope in the world and live in Botswana.
Lechwe gather in large herds on the Okavango and Chobe floodplains.
The African wildcat, ancestor of house cats, lives in Botswana.
Painted reed frogs call loudly from the Okavango's reeds at night.
Hippos are among the most dangerous animals in Africa.
The puff adder is a common, well-camouflaged snake in Botswana.
Scorpions glow under ultraviolet light, which helps researchers find them at night.
Elephants in Botswana travel long distances between the rivers and the Kalahari.
Botswana banned commercial trophy hunting in 2014 and lifted the ban in 2019.
A group of lions is called a pride; a group of meerkats is a mob.
Wild dogs have one of the highest hunting success rates of any predator.
The Kalahari lion can survive long periods without drinking water.
The southern ground hornbill walks the grasslands hunting small animals.
More than 550 bird species have been recorded in Botswana.
The lilac-breasted roller is one of Botswana's most photographed birds.
The African fish eagle's call is one of the classic sounds of the Okavango.
Pel's fishing owl, a rare giant owl, hunts fish at night along the Okavango Panhandle.
The wattled crane, a threatened species, breeds in the Okavango.
Southern carmine bee-eaters nest in colonies in riverbanks in northern Botswana.
The African skimmer flies low over the water with its lower bill slicing the surface.
The slaty egret is a rare heron found in the Okavango.
Saddle-billed storks have a bright red and black bill with a yellow saddle.
The ostrich, the world's largest bird, roams the Kalahari and the pans.
Sociable weavers build huge shared nests that can house hundreds of birds.
Red-billed quelea flocks can number in the millions.
The secretary bird stamps on snakes and lizards to kill them.
The African jacana walks on lily pads with very long toes.
Jacana fathers raise the chicks and can carry them under their wings.
The hamerkop builds an enormous dome-shaped nest of sticks.
Marabou storks are often seen around carcasses and dumps.
Vultures help keep the bush clean by eating carcasses.
Poisoning by poachers has killed many vultures in Botswana.
The yellow-billed hornbill is nicknamed the flying banana.
Hornbill females seal themselves inside a tree hole while nesting.
The grey go-away-bird is named after its call.
Pied kingfishers hover above water before diving for fish.
The malachite kingfisher is tiny and brilliantly coloured.
The goliath heron is the largest heron in the world and lives in the Okavango.
The white-backed vulture is critically endangered.
The bateleur eagle tilts from side to side as it glides.
Guineafowl move in noisy flocks through Botswana's bush.
The kori bustard male puffs out its neck feathers in courtship.
The red-billed oxpecker eats ticks off giraffes, buffalo and other large animals.
The Okavango is an Important Bird Area for many water birds.
The southern yellow-billed hornbill and red-billed hornbill are common in Botswana.
Openbill storks use their gapped bills to eat snails.
Crimson-breasted shrikes are often seen in the Kalahari's acacia scrub.
Pale chanting goshawks perch on trees across the Kalahari.
The baobab (mowana) can live for more than a thousand years.
Baobabs store water in their huge, swollen trunks.
The mopane tree has butterfly-shaped leaves.
Mopane woodland covers large parts of northern Botswana.
Marula (morula) fruit is eaten fresh and used to make drinks and jam.
Marula trees are either male or female; only females bear fruit.
Devil's claw (sengaparile) is a Kalahari plant used in traditional medicine.
The sausage tree (moporota) has heavy fruit that look like sausages.
Mokoro canoes were traditionally carved from sausage trees or African ebony.
Wild sour plums (moretologa) grow in the Kalahari.
The camelthorn (mogotlho) has seed pods eaten by many animals.
Motlopi (shepherd's tree) gives shade and its roots are used as a coffee substitute.
The mophane tree is used for firewood, building poles and fences.
Grapple plants have hooked seeds that catch on animals' feet.
The Kalahari's tsamma melons and gemsbok cucumbers are important water sources.
Papyrus grows up to several metres tall in the Okavango.
Real fan palms (mokola) dot the islands of the Okavango.
The African ebony (motlhakola) grows on Okavango islands.
Leadwood trees are so dense that their wood sinks in water.
The wild date palm grows on islands in the Okavango.
The morama bean is a Kalahari plant with edible seeds and tubers.
Hoodia, a cactus-like Kalahari plant, was traditionally chewed by the San to stave off hunger.
The San (Basarwa) are the oldest inhabitants of Botswana and southern Africa.
The Tsodilo Hills hold evidence of human activity going back many thousands of years.
Iron Age farmers lived in eastern Botswana more than a thousand years ago.
Toutswe, in eastern Botswana, was a major cattle-keeping settlement around 1,000 years ago.
Botswana became a British protectorate, Bechuanaland, in 1885.
The Bechuanaland Protectorate was run from Mafikeng, a town outside its own borders, in South Africa.
In 1895 Kgosi Khama III, Sebele I and Bathoen I went to London to keep their land from Cecil Rhodes's company.
The three dikgosi met Queen Victoria in 1895 and Britain kept the protectorate out of Rhodes's hands.
The Jameson Raid of 1895 into the Transvaal was launched from Pitsani, in the Bechuanaland Protectorate.
David Livingstone set up a mission at Kolobeng, near Gaborone, in 1847.
Kgosi Sechele I of the Bakwena was baptised by David Livingstone.
The ruins of Livingstone's Kolobeng mission are a national monument.
Missionary Robert Moffat completed a full Setswana Bible translation in 1857.
Khama III ruled the Bangwato from 1875 until his death in 1923.
Khama III was a Christian ruler who banned alcohol in his territory.
Khama III moved his capital from Shoshong to Palapye in 1889 and then to Serowe in 1902.
Shoshong was the capital of the Bangwato in the 19th century.
The Battle of Dimawe in 1852 saw Batswana resist Boer raiders.
Tshekedi Khama ruled as regent for his nephew Seretse after 1925.
Many Batswana soldiers served with the African Pioneer Corps in the Second World War.
In 1943 a troopship, the SS Erinpura, sank with the loss of many Batswana soldiers.
The Bechuanaland Democratic Party, later the BDP, was founded in 1962.
The first general election under universal adult suffrage was held in 1965.
Seretse Khama became Prime Minister of Bechuanaland in 1965.
Botswana became independent on 30 September 1966.
At independence in 1966 Botswana was one of the poorest countries in the world.
Gaborone became the capital in 1965, replacing Mafikeng.
Gaborone was built as a planned capital in the 1960s.
Diamonds were discovered at Orapa in 1967, a year after independence.
Botswana introduced its own currency, the pula, in 1976.
Before 1976 Botswana used the South African rand.
The Botswana Defence Force was founded in 1977.
Botswana was a founding member of SADCC, now SADC, in 1980.
Sir Seretse Khama died in office on 13 July 1980.
The University of Botswana became a full national university in 1982.
Botswana has held regular multi-party elections since independence.
In 2024 the Umbrella for Democratic Change won the election, ending 58 years of BDP rule.
Batswana fought colonial plans to hand the protectorate to South Africa.
Britain's High Commissioner in South Africa oversaw the Bechuanaland Protectorate.
The Bechuanaland Protectorate's railway line was built in the 1890s to link Mafikeng with Bulawayo.
Francistown grew from a gold rush in the late 1860s and 1870s at Tati.
The Tati Concession around Francistown was an early gold mining area.
The Bechuanaland Protectorate was split from British Bechuanaland, a colony that became part of the Cape in 1895.
Bechuanaland stamps were first overprinted British and Cape stamps.
The name Botswana means "land of the Tswana".
The national monument at Domboshaba in north-east Botswana is a stone ruin linked to Great Zimbabwe.
Botswana opened its first diamond mine at Orapa in 1971.
Botswana's National Museum in Gaborone opened in 1968.
Sir Seretse Khama was born in Serowe in 1921.
Seretse Khama studied at Fort Hare in South Africa and Balliol College, Oxford.
Seretse Khama married Ruth Williams, an Englishwoman, in London in 1948.
Britain exiled Seretse Khama from 1950 to 1956 under pressure from apartheid South Africa.
Seretse Khama returned to Bechuanaland in 1956 after giving up his claim to the chieftainship.
Seretse Khama was Botswana's first president, from 1966 to 1980.
Seretse Khama was knighted in 1966.
Sir Seretse Khama International Airport in Gaborone is named after him.
The 2016 film A United Kingdom tells the story of Seretse and Ruth Khama.
In A United Kingdom, Seretse Khama is played by David Oyelowo and Ruth by Rosamund Pike.
Ruth Williams Khama became Botswana's first First Lady.
Ruth Khama was known in Botswana as Mohumagadi Mma Kgosi.
Ruth Williams Khama died in 2002 and is buried beside Seretse in Serowe.
Sir Seretse Khama Day is a public holiday on 1 July.
Seretse Khama pushed for non-racial government from the very start of independence.
Seretse Khama's government used diamond income to build schools, roads and clinics.
The royal cemetery on Serowe's hill holds the graves of Khama III and Seretse Khama.
Seretse Khama's statue stands in front of the National Assembly in Gaborone.
The book Colour Bar by Susan Williams tells the story of Seretse and Ruth.
Botswana is a parliamentary republic whose president is elected by the National Assembly.
Sir Ketumile Masire was Botswana's second president, from 1980 to 1998.
Festus Mogae was Botswana's third president, from 1998 to 2008.
Festus Mogae won the Ibrahim Prize for Achievement in African Leadership in 2008.
Ian Khama was Botswana's fourth president, from 2008 to 2018.
Mokgweetsi Masisi was Botswana's fifth president, from 2018 to 2024.
Duma Boko became Botswana's sixth president in November 2024.
Botswana's presidents are limited to two five-year terms.
Botswana's parliament is the National Assembly; elections are held every five years.
Ntlo ya Dikgosi (House of Chiefs) advises parliament on customary and tribal matters.
Botswana's constitution came into force at independence in 1966.
The kgotla is a traditional community assembly where anyone may speak.
Kgotla meetings are usually held under a tree or in an open enclosure.
Customary courts at the kgotla still handle many local disputes.
Botswana is often ranked among Africa's least corrupt countries.
Botswana's High Court has its main seat in Lobatse and also sits in Gaborone and Francistown.
Botswana's Court of Appeal is the country's highest court.
Botswana's capital Gaborone hosts the headquarters of SADC.
Botswana is a member of the Commonwealth, the African Union and the United Nations.
The Directorate on Corruption and Economic Crime was set up in 1994.
In 2019 Botswana's High Court decriminalised same-sex relationships.
Botswana's official language is English and its national language is Setswana.
Unity Dow won a 1992 case that let Botswana women pass citizenship to their children.
Unity Dow became Botswana's first woman High Court judge in 1998.
Dr Gaositwe Chiepe was Botswana's first woman cabinet minister.
Botswana's national anthem is Fatshe leno la rona ("This land of ours").
The national anthem was written and composed by Kgalemang Tumediso Motsete.
Botswana's motto, on the coat of arms, is "Pula", meaning rain.
Botswana's coat of arms shows two zebras holding an elephant tusk and a sorghum stalk.
The blue of Botswana's flag stands for water and rain.
The black and white stripes of Botswana's flag stand for racial harmony and recall the zebra.
Botswana's flag was adopted at independence in 1966.
The three cogwheels on Botswana's coat of arms stand for industry.
The waves on Botswana's coat of arms stand for water.
The bull's head on Botswana's coat of arms stands for cattle farming.
Botswana's main tribal groups include the Bangwato, Bakwena, Bangwaketse, Batawana, Bakgatla, Balete, Barolong and Batlokwa.
Dikgosi (chiefs) remain important leaders in Botswana's villages.
Botswana's first president's party, the BDP, ruled from 1966 to 2024.
Setswana is spoken by most people in Botswana and by millions in South Africa.
Setswana is one of South Africa's official languages.
In Setswana, one person is a Motswana and the people are Batswana.
"Dumela" means hello in Setswana; "Dumelang" greets several people.
"Ke a leboga" means thank you in Setswana.
"Tsamaya sentle" means go well, said to someone leaving.
"Sala sentle" means stay well, said by the person leaving.
"O tsogile jang?" is a Setswana morning greeting: how did you wake up?
"Ke tsogile sentle" means I woke up well.
"Rra" is used to address a man and "Mma" to address a woman respectfully.
"Pula" means rain in Setswana, and it is also the name of Botswana's currency.
"Thebe" means shield; 100 thebe make one pula.
"Kgosi" means chief or king in Setswana.
"Motse" means village or town in Setswana.
"Metsi" means water in Setswana.
"Ntlo" means house in Setswana.
"Kgomo" means cow, and "dikgomo" means cattle.
"Letsatsi" means both sun and day in Setswana.
"Ngwedi" means moon and month in Setswana.
"Naledi" means star in Setswana and is also a popular name.
"Tau" means lion in Setswana.
"Tlou" means elephant in Setswana.
"Nkwe" means leopard in Setswana.
"Phiri" means hyena in Setswana.
"Thutlwa" means giraffe in Setswana.
"Kwena" means crocodile; it is the totem of the Bakwena.
"Tshwene" means baboon in Setswana.
"Noga" means snake in Setswana.
"Nonyane" means bird in Setswana.
"Tshukudu" means rhino in Setswana.
"Nare" means buffalo in Setswana.
"Tholo" means kudu in Setswana.
"Phala" means impala in Setswana.
"Kgama" means red hartebeest, which gave the Khama family its name.
"Pitse" means horse, and a zebra is "pitse ya naga", the horse of the veld.
"Mowana" means baobab in Setswana.
"Lefatshe" means land or country in Setswana.
"Sekolo" means school in Setswana.
"Bana" means children in Setswana.
"Mosadi" means woman and "monna" means man in Setswana.
"Mme" means mother and "rre" means father in Setswana.
"Nko" means nose and "matlho" means eyes in Setswana.
"Dijo" means food in Setswana.
"Ee" means yes and "nnyaa" means no in Setswana.
"Ke a go rata" means I love you in Setswana.
"Go siame" means it's alright in Setswana.
Setswana counts: nngwe (1), pedi (2), tharo (3), nne (4), tlhano (5).
Six to ten in Setswana: thataro, supa, robedi, robongwe, lesome.
Monday in Setswana is Mosupologo.
Tuesday is Labobedi, the "second day", in Setswana.
Wednesday is Laboraro, the "third day", in Setswana.
Thursday is Labone, the "fourth day", in Setswana.
Friday is Labotlhano, the "fifth day", in Setswana.
Saturday is Matlhatso in Setswana.
Sunday is Tshipi in Setswana.
January in Setswana is Ferikgong.
February in Setswana is Tlhakole.
March in Setswana is Mopitlwe.
April in Setswana is Moranang.
May in Setswana is Motsheganong.
June in Setswana is Seetebosigo.
July in Setswana is Phukwi.
August in Setswana is Phatwe.
September in Setswana is Lwetse.
October in Setswana is Diphalane.
November in Setswana is Ngwanatsele.
December in Setswana is Sedimonthole.
Setswana is a Bantu language closely related to Sesotho and Sepedi.
Setswana nouns come in classes marked by prefixes, like mo- for one person and ba- for many.
Many Setswana place names end in "-ng", a suffix meaning "at" a place, as in Jwaneng.
Setswana uses the letter "g" for a sound like the "ch" in Scottish "loch".
Solomon Plaatje translated Shakespeare into Setswana in the 1930s.
Sol Plaatje wrote Mhudi, one of the first novels in English by a black South African, and he was a Motswana.
A Setswana proverb says "Kgosi ke kgosi ka batho": a chief is a chief through the people.
A Setswana proverb says "Kgetsi ya tsie e kgonwa ka go tshwaraganelwa": a bag of locusts is lifted together.
"Mmangwana o tshwara thipa ka fa bogaleng" says a mother holds the knife by the sharp edge, to protect her child.
"Ntwa kgolo ke ya molomo" means the greatest battle is fought with words.
"Moeng goroga re je ka wena" welcomes guests: arrive, visitor, so we may eat because of you.
"Botho" is the Setswana idea of humanity, respect and caring for others.
Botho is one of the pillars of Botswana's national Vision 2016 and Vision 2036.
"Pula!" is shouted at gatherings in Botswana as a blessing and cheer.
Many Batswana names have meanings, like Kagiso (peace), Lesedi (light) and Mpho (gift).
The name Tumelo means faith and Boitumelo means joy in Setswana.
Setswana praise poetry is called maboko.
Seswaa, slow-boiled and pounded beef or goat, is Botswana's national dish.
Seswaa is traditionally cooked by men in three-legged pots at weddings and funerals.
Bogobe is a stiff porridge made from sorghum or maize.
Bogobe jwa lerotse is porridge cooked with lerotse, a type of melon.
Morogo is wild spinach, often cooked with onion and tomato.
Phane (mopane worms) are dried and eaten as a crunchy, protein-rich snack.
Phane harvesting is an important seasonal income in rural Botswana.
Madila is a thick sour milk often eaten with bogobe.
Magwinya are fat cakes, deep-fried dough balls sold at roadside stalls.
Dikgobe is a mix of samp or sorghum with beans.
Serobe is a dish of tripe and intestines, often cooked at celebrations.
Mabele is the Setswana word for sorghum, a staple grain of Botswana.
Ting is a fermented sorghum porridge with a sour taste.
Bojalwa jwa Setswana is a traditional sorghum beer.
Mageu (motogo) is a soured maize or sorghum drink.
Botswana beef is exported to Europe and other markets.
The Botswana Meat Commission abattoir in Lobatse opened in 1954.
Morula fruit can be made into a fermented drink.
Leputshe is a kind of pumpkin cooked in Botswana.
Diphaphata are flat, round breads cooked on a pan, a favourite Botswana breakfast.
Mosutlho is samp, the coarse crushed maize often cooked with beans.
Letlhodi are mung beans, popular in Botswana cooking.
Seswaa is often served with bogobe and morogo.
Masonja is another name for mopane worms in parts of southern Africa.
Wild melons called tsamma are eaten and stored by people in the Kalahari.
Mokoro tours often end with a bush picnic on an Okavango island.
Seswaa is cooked with salt and little else, letting the meat speak for itself.
Cattle are a traditional sign of wealth in Botswana.
Bogadi is the Setswana bride price, traditionally paid in cattle.
Many Batswana families keep a cattle post (moraka) far from their home village.
Many Batswana have a home village, a cattle post and fields (masimo).
Morabaraba, a twelve-cow mill game, is played across Botswana and southern Africa.
Diketo is a stone-throwing game children play with a hole in the ground.
Mmele is another name for the mill game played in Botswana.
Moruba (also called Nsolo) is a four-row mancala game played in southern Africa.
Okavango baskets are woven from mokola palm leaves and dyed with natural colours.
Basket patterns in the Okavango have names like "Tears of the Giraffe" and "Flight of the Swallow".
Etsha villages in the Okavango are famous for their Hambukushu basket weavers.
Gumare is another Okavango village known for fine baskets.
Thamaga is known for its pottery, made with local clay.
Oodi weavers near Gaborone have made tapestries since the 1970s.
Lentswe la Oodi weavers' tapestries show village life in bright colours.
Botswana's San communities make ostrich eggshell beads.
Ostrich eggshell beads are among the oldest kinds of jewellery in the world.
The Kuru Art Project in D'Kar has made San artists known worldwide.
Traditional Batswana homes (rondavels) have round mud walls and thatched roofs.
Lelapa is the courtyard of a traditional Setswana home, often smoothed with mud and dung.
Women traditionally decorate home walls with patterns called lekgapho.
Mokgatlho is a Setswana word for an association or cooperative.
Letsema is a Setswana tradition of working together in the fields.
Boipelego means self-reliance, an idea at the heart of Botswana's development.
Initiation schools called bogwera (for boys) and bojale (for girls) were part of Setswana tradition.
Age regiments (mephato) were once formed during initiation.
Totems (diano) link families and clans with an animal such as the crocodile or elephant.
The Bangwato totem is the duiker (phuti).
The Bakgatla totem is the monkey (kgabo).
The Barolong totem is the kudu (tholo).
Wedding celebrations in Botswana often last several days.
Mourners in Botswana traditionally share a meal of seswaa after a funeral.
The German print fabric called leteisi is a favourite for Botswana women's dresses.
Wedding guests in Botswana often wear matching leteisi outfits.
Batswana elders are greeted first and with respect.
Parents in Botswana are often called after their first child, such as Mma Kagiso (Kagiso's mother).
Many Batswana names honour events at birth, such as Pula for a child born in the rain.
Bessie Head wrote her novels in the village of Serowe.
Bessie Head's novels include When Rain Clouds Gather, Maru and A Question of Power.
Bessie Head's Serowe: Village of the Rain Wind tells the village's history.
The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency books by Alexander McCall Smith are set in Gaborone.
Mma Precious Ramotswe is the detective in The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency.
The No. 1 Ladies' Detective Agency TV series was filmed in Botswana.
Unity Dow is also a novelist; her books include The Screaming of the Innocent.
Thapong Visual Arts Centre in Gaborone supports local artists.
The Phuthadikobo Museum in Mochudi is housed in an old school building.
The Khama III Memorial Museum is in Serowe.
The Supa Ngwao Museum is in Francistown.
The Kgosi Bathoen II Museum is in Kanye.
Rock art in the Tsodilo Hills was made by San and other peoples.
Traditional dances in Botswana include borankana, phathisi and setapa.
Setapa is a traditional dance of the Bangwaketse.
Tsutsube is a San healing and trance dance.
The segaba is a one-stringed fiddle used in Setswana music.
The setinkane is a thumb piano played in Botswana.
Kwasa kwasa, a Congolese rumba style, became hugely popular in Botswana.
Franco and Afro Musica made kwasa kwasa a Botswana favourite.
Culture Spears is a Botswana band known for traditional music.
Vee Mampeezy is a Botswana star of kwasa kwasa and house.
Botswana has a strong gospel music scene.
Choirs singing in Setswana are popular at church and school events.
Botswana metal fans, known as "renegades", dress in black leather and cowboy hats.
Botswana's heavy metal fans have been featured in photo books and documentaries.
Hip-hop and house music, known locally as "motswako", mix Setswana and English.
Motswako is a rap style mixing Setswana, English and other languages.
Phathisi is a dance performed by men with clapping and leg slapping.
Dikhwaere (choral music) competitions are held across Botswana.
Drums and hand claps drive many traditional Setswana dances.
The Maitisong Festival is an arts festival held in Gaborone.
Botswana Day (Independence Day) is celebrated on 30 September.
1 October is also a public holiday in Botswana, after Botswana Day.
President's Day in July is a public holiday with dance and music competitions.
Labour Day on 1 May is a public holiday in Botswana.
The Kuru Dance Festival at D'Kar celebrates San culture.
The Domboshaba Festival celebrates the Kalanga culture of north-east Botswana.
The Dithubaruba Cultural Festival celebrates the Bakwena heritage.
The Khawa Dune Challenge is a festival of desert racing and culture in the Kgalagadi.
The Toyota Desert Race was held near Jwaneng for many years.
The Maun International Arts Festival celebrates Okavango art.
Christmas is a public holiday in Botswana, as is Boxing Day.
Good Friday and Easter Monday are public holidays in Botswana.
The Ascension Day public holiday falls on a Thursday in Botswana.
New Year's Day is followed by a second public holiday on 2 January.
Botswana's Independence anniversary celebrations take place at the National Stadium in Gaborone.
Botswana is one of the world's largest diamond producers by value.
Debswana is a 50-50 partnership between the Botswana government and De Beers.
Jwaneng is often called the world's richest diamond mine by value.
Jwaneng diamond mine opened in 1982.
Orapa is one of the largest diamond mines in the world by area.
Orapa is a closed town run by the mining company.
Letlhakane mine, near Orapa, began production in 1977.
The Karowe mine found the 1,111-carat Lesedi La Rona diamond in 2015.
Lesedi La Rona means "our light" in Setswana.
The 1,758-carat Sewelô diamond was found at Karowe in 2019.
A 2,492-carat diamond, the second largest ever found, was found at Karowe in 2024.
Sewelô means "rare find" in Setswana.
De Beers moved its global diamond sales from London to Gaborone in 2013.
The Okavango Diamond Company sells a share of Botswana's diamonds.
Diamonds paid for much of Botswana's schools, roads and hospitals.
Botswana grew from one of the poorest countries to upper-middle-income status.
Botswana's economy grew very fast for decades after independence.
The Pula Fund is Botswana's sovereign wealth fund, built from diamond income.
The Bank of Botswana was founded in 1975.
The Botswana Stock Exchange in Gaborone traces its roots to 1989.
Copper is mined in Botswana's Kalahari Copperbelt around Ghanzi.
Selebi-Phikwe's copper-nickel mine closed in 2016.
Morupule, near Palapye, is Botswana's coal mine and power station.
Botswana has huge coal reserves, much of them still untouched.
Tourism is one of Botswana's biggest earners after diamonds.
Botswana's tourism focuses on high-value, low-volume safaris.
Cattle ranching is an important part of Botswana's rural economy.
Botswana's beef is traceable thanks to cattle ear tags and boluses.
Air Botswana, the national airline, was founded in 1972.
Botswana Railways runs the line from Ramatlabama to Francistown and beyond.
The Trans-Kalahari Highway links Botswana with Namibia's coast.
Botswana's pula notes show animals, people and the national coat of arms.
The 5 thebe coin once showed a toko (hornbill).
The pula is pegged to a basket of currencies, including the rand.
Diamond cutting and polishing factories have opened in Gaborone.
The Diamond Technology Park in Gaborone hosts diamond cutting firms.
Solar power is expanding thanks to Botswana's strong sunshine.
Gaborone is Botswana's capital and largest city.
Gaborone is named after Kgosi Gaborone of the Batlokwa.
Gaborone was once known as Gaberones.
Gaborone's name changed from Gaberones in 1969.
The Three Dikgosi Monument in Gaborone shows Khama III, Sebele I and Bathoen I.
The Three Dikgosi Monument was unveiled in 2005.
Gaborone's Main Mall is one of the city's oldest shopping streets.
Kgale Hill, the "Sleeping Giant", overlooks Gaborone.
Mokolodi Nature Reserve lies just south of Gaborone.
Gaborone Game Reserve is a small reserve inside the city.
Francistown is Botswana's second-largest city.
Francistown is sometimes called the Capital of the North.
Maun was founded as the capital of the BaTawana in 1915.
Maun's name comes from a San word meaning "place of short reeds".
Kasane sits where the Chobe River meets the Zambezi.
Serowe is one of Botswana's largest villages and the home of the Bangwato.
Molepolole is the main village of the Bakwena.
Kanye is the main village of the Bangwaketse.
Mochudi is the main village of the Bakgatla.
Ramotswa is the main village of the Balete.
Mogoditshane, beside Gaborone, is one of Botswana's fastest-growing villages.
Tlokweng is the home of the Batlokwa, just east of Gaborone.
Palapye is home to the Botswana International University of Science and Technology.
Mahalapye is a railway town between Gaborone and Francistown.
Selebi-Phikwe was built in the 1970s as a copper-nickel mining town.

Ghanzi is known as the capital of the Kalahari.
Tsabong is the main town of the Kgalagadi District.
Shakawe sits on the Okavango Panhandle near the Namibian border.
Gumare lies on the western edge of the Okavango Delta.
Nata is a crossroads village on the way to Kasane and Maun.
Letlhakane is a mining village near Orapa.
Tonota is a village near Francistown on the Shashe River.
Lobatse was once the seat of the High Court of the Bechuanaland Protectorate.
Mmamashia, north of Gaborone, has water treatment works for the capital.

Martin's Drift is a border crossing over the Limpopo.
Kazungula is a border crossing to Zambia, now with a road and rail bridge.
Mamuno is the main border post with Namibia on the Trans-Kalahari Highway.
Ngoma Bridge crosses the Chobe River into Namibia.
Gaborone's Parliament buildings were built in the 1960s.
Old Palapye's ruins include the church built by Khama III.
Botswana has two UNESCO World Heritage Sites: the Tsodilo Hills and the Okavango Delta.
The Tsodilo Hills were listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001.
The Tsodilo Hills have over 4,500 rock paintings in about 10 km².
The Tsodilo Hills are called the "Louvre of the Desert".
The San call Tsodilo's main hills the Male, the Female and the Child.
Tsodilo is a sacred place for the San and Hambukushu peoples.
A rock at Tsodilo has been described as looking like a python, and some see it as a very old ritual site.
Tsodilo's paintings include eland, giraffe, rhino and human figures.
Domboshaba ruins near Francistown date from the time of the Zimbabwe culture.
Matsieng, near Rasesa, has rock carvings of footprints said to be from the first human.
The Matsieng footprints are a national monument.
Kgosi Sechele I Museum in Molepolole celebrates the Bakwena leader.
Khama III's grave is on the royal hill in Serowe.
The ruins of Old Palapye are a national monument.
The Gcwihaba Caves are a national monument.
The Manyana rock paintings are a national monument.
The Tsodilo Hills are on the edge of the Okavango Panhandle in the Ngamiland District.

Botswana's women's football team is nicknamed the Mares.

Township Rollers is one of Botswana's most successful football clubs.
The National Stadium in Gaborone is Botswana's main sports venue.
Botswana's athletics team has become one of Africa's strongest in sprints.
Netball is a popular sport for girls in Botswana.
Softball is played widely in Botswana schools.
Basketball and volleyball are growing sports in Botswana.
Morabaraba is recognised as a sport by Mind Sports South Africa.
Desert racing and quad biking are popular in the Kalahari.
The Botswana Premier League is the top football league.

Letsile Tebogo was the 2022 World U20 100 m champion.

Lesedi La Rona was the largest diamond found in more than a century when it was discovered.

The Central Kalahari Game Reserve is one of the largest game reserves in the world.
